prompt: You need to change some upstream Chromium behavior and can't do it purely within brave-core. In what order of preference should you reach for options?
choices: A patch first, since it's the most explicit and reviewable, then chromium_src
Brave-only code, then chromium_src, then a patch as last resort
chromium_src and patches are equally fine; pick whichever is shorter
Edit `src/` directly and skip generating patch files
explain: Avoid modifying Chromium whenever possible. When unavoidable, chromium_src overrides are strongly preferred; patches (generated with `pnpm run update_patches`) are the last resort and should be minimal.

prompt:
An upstream test fails in Brave because of an intentional behavior change. A PR adds this to a chromium_src override:

```cpp
#define SomeUpstreamTest DISABLED_SomeUpstreamTest
```

What should the reviewer request?
choices: Disable it via a `test/filters/` file and keep Brave's version in a Brave test target
Fine — `#define`-renaming to `DISABLED_` is the standard way to disable upstream tests
Keep the `#define` but add an `#undef` after the include so it doesn't leak
Patch the upstream test file to add `DISABLED_` instead
explain: Never disable upstream tests via `#define ... DISABLED_...` in chromium_src. Use filter files in `test/filters/`, and move Brave-specific replacements into `brave_unit_tests`, `brave_browser_tests`, etc.

prompt: You need different color logic in `ChromeTypographyProvider::GetColor` only when `ShouldIgnoreHarmonySpec()` is false. Which override shape is preferred?
choices: Copy the full 50-line upstream function and edit the 3 lines that differ
Patch upstream `GetColor` with an `if` block that calls into Brave code
Return `ChromiumImpl::GetColor(...)` unless the condition applies
Replace the whole class with a dummy no-op implementation
explain: Minimize duplication in overrides: wrap only the changed section and fall back to `ChromiumImpl` for everything else.

prompt: An upstream `.cc` file needs to `#include "brave/components/my_feature/my_header.h"`. A PR does this by adding a one-line patch. What's preferred?
choices: A one-line patch is ideal; keep it
Add the header to the upstream target's `public_deps` via a GN arg
Copy the upstream file into brave-core and include it there
Add the include via a chromium_src override
explain: Always prefer a chromium_src override over a patch — patches are harder to maintain, conflict more, and are harder to review. Required headers should be added through chromium_src, not patches.

prompt: A chromium_src override reproduces an entire 60-line upstream method because 3 lines need to change. What's the standard?
choices: Acceptable if the copied code has a comment marking the changed lines
Copy the whole file instead, so the method stays consistent with its neighbors
Acceptable as long as `check_chromium_src.py` passes
Override only the changed part; call the original for the rest
explain: Never copy entire Chromium files or methods into chromium_src. Override only what needs to change and delegate to the superclass for everything else.

prompt: You need `TabStrip` to create a `BraveNewTabButton` instead of `NewTabButton`. Which approach follows the standard?
choices: Patch `tab_strip.cc` to construct `BraveNewTabButton` directly
Patch every method of `NewTabButton` that needs Brave behavior
A chromium_src `#define NewTabButton BraveNewTabButton`
Copy `tab_strip.cc` into chromium_src with the one-line change applied
explain: Prefer subclassing over patching, in both C++ and Java. Swapping in a Brave subclass via chromium_src (or one patch changing a superclass in Java) is easier to maintain than patching individual methods.

prompt: Inside a chromium_src override, which include is correct?
choices: `#include "brave/chromium_src/net/proxy_resolution/proxy_resolution_service.h"`
`#include "net/proxy_resolution/proxy_resolution_service.h"`
`#include "../../../net/proxy_resolution/proxy_resolution_service.h"`
`#include "chromium_src/net/proxy_resolution/proxy_resolution_service.h"`
explain: In chromium_src overrides, always include the original header path, never the chromium_src version.

prompt: Brave wants to fully disable `TranslateURLFetcher`. A PR adds two patches (one for the `.h`, one for the `.cc`). What's the preferred approach?
choices: Dummy no-op `.h`/`.cc` replacements in chromium_src
Keep the two patches but combine them into one
Add `#define TranslateURLFetcher BraveTranslateURLFetcher` and subclass it
Remove the class from the upstream BUILD.gn via a GN patch
explain: To disable or replace a Chromium class entirely, add minimal no-op dummy replacements in chromium_src for the `.h` and `.cc` — no patch needed and easier maintenance.

prompt: You need `SomeClass::SomeMethod` to be virtual so a Brave subclass can override it. Which approach is correct?
choices: A plaster rewrite with `make_virtual`
`#define SomeMethod virtual SomeMethod` around the upstream header include
`#define final` around the upstream include
Subclass and hide the method with a same-named non-virtual one
explain: Don't use `#define` to add `virtual` — it rewrites every `SomeMethod` in the translation unit. Use the `make_virtual` plaster rewriter, which also handles pointer/reference return types and destructors.

prompt:
```cpp
#define final
#include "src/chrome/browser/ui/views/side_panel/side_panel_coordinator.h"
#undef final
```

What's the reviewer's verdict?
choices: Accept, since the `#undef` immediately limits the scope
Accept if `final` appears only once in that header and nowhere in its includes
Replace it with `#define final override`
Reject: it's undefined behavior and viral
explain: Never `#define final` — it's undefined behavior per the C++ standard and can break unrelated code using `final`. Use a minimal patch to remove `final` or find another approach.

prompt: A new chromium_src override replaces `TabView::BuildContextMenu()`. A per-function comment already explains it adds Brave menu items because upstream isn't extensible there. A reviewer also asks for a file-level comment. Correct?
choices: Yes — every override file needs a file-level header comment
Yes — and each method injected via `#define` also needs its own doc comment
No — per-function comments are enough
No — chromium_src overrides should never have comments
explain: chromium_src overrides should explain why they're needed, but a file-level comment isn't required if per-function comments cover it. Don't ask for doc comments inside `#define` macro bodies either.

prompt: You add a new `#include` of a Brave header to a chromium_src override. How do you verify the dependency is wired up?
choices: If it compiles locally, the dependency is fine
Add the include to the upstream file temporarily and run `gn check`
Run `check_chromium_src.py`, which validates GN deps for override includes
Add the header to `brave/BUILD.gn` `public_deps` to be safe
explain: The override compiles as part of the upstream target, which may lack deps on your headers. Test by adding the include to the upstream file and running `gn check`; if it fails, the dep must be added.

prompt: A chromium_src override of `window_feature_controller.cc` includes `brave/browser/ui/views/tabs/vertical_tab_utils.h`, and a patch adds `//brave/browser/ui/views/tabs` to the upstream target's deps. What's the preferred design?
choices: Keep the include but move the GN dependency into `sources.gni` instead of a patch
Keep it; a single Brave include in an override is acceptable
Forward-declare a hook in the override; implement it in a Brave target
Copy `vertical_tab_utils.h` into chromium_src so no dep is needed
explain: chromium_src should avoid depending on `//brave/...` targets — that creates an upstream→Brave dep. Forward-declare a hook in the override, implement it in a dedicated Brave target, and have a top-level Brave target depend on it.

prompt:
In a chromium_src override you see:

```cpp
provider_ = nullptr;
```

with no context. What should the reviewer ask for?
choices: Replace it with `provider_.reset()` so the ownership is explicit
Remove it — upstream code will null the pointer during shutdown anyway
Wrap it in `DCHECK(provider_)` first
A comment explaining why it's reset, e.g. to avoid a dangling pointer
explain: Add comments for non-obvious `nullptr` assignments in chromium_src — the override is out of context from the original file, so intent (like dangling-pointer prevention) isn't clear.

prompt: You add `constexpr int kBravePolicySource = 10;` after upstream's `POLICY_SOURCE_COUNT`. What protects against upstream adding values?
choices: A `DCHECK` at startup comparing upstream's count with `kBravePolicySource`
A `static_assert` that the upstream count is `<= kBravePolicySource`
Choosing a large value like `1000` so clashes are unlikely
A unit test that logs the enum count
explain: When appending custom values after an upstream enum, add a `static_assert` so the build fails if upstream grows the enum and values would clash.

prompt: You're adding a Brave-specific Blink runtime-enabled feature `BraveGlobalPrivacyControl`. Where does it go?
choices: `runtime_enabled_features.override.json5`
A patch to `runtime_enabled_features.json5`
A chromium_src override of `runtime_enabled_features.cc`
A new `base::Feature` in `brave/components/` only
explain: Add Brave Blink runtime-enabled features to `runtime_enabled_features.override.json5` — it's designed for downstream additions and avoids patch conflicts with `runtime_enabled_features.json5`.

prompt: You need to change `PrivateHelper()`, defined in an anonymous namespace in upstream `chrome/browser/feature.cc`. How?
choices: Use a `.patch` file
A chromium_src override that `#define`s `PrivateHelper` to a Brave function
Subclass the file's class and override `PrivateHelper`
Use `make_virtual` on `PrivateHelper`
explain: chromium_src overrides only work for symbols with external linkage. Static or anonymous-namespace functions in upstream `.cc` files aren't visible outside the TU, so use a patch.

prompt: Upstream calls `l10n_util::GetStringFUTF16(IDS_FOO, site_name)` (one `$1`). You `#define` `IDS_FOO` to `IDS_BRAVE_FOO`. What must be true of `IDS_BRAVE_FOO`?
choices: It must have no placeholders at all
Any placeholders are fine; extra ones are filled with empty strings
Its placeholders must be compatible with the upstream caller's
It must have at least two placeholders for flexibility
explain: Replacement strings must match the placeholders the upstream caller provides. Fewer are silently ignored; more or different ones can cause runtime errors.

prompt:
You're reviewing a chromium_src override that swaps an upstream string:

```cpp
#undef IDS_PASSWORD_MANAGER_UI_EMPTY_STATE_SYNCING_USERS
#define IDS_PASSWORD_MANAGER_UI_EMPTY_STATE_SYNCING_USERS \
  IDS_BRAVE_PASSWORD_MANAGER_UI_EMPTY_STATE
```

What should be added?
choices: Nothing — `check_chromium_src.py` already makes any extra guard redundant
An `#ifndef`/`#error` guard before the `#undef`
Wrap the `#undef` in `#if defined(...)` so it's skipped if the ID disappears
A runtime `DCHECK` that the string resource loads successfully
explain: Guard overridden string IDs with `#ifndef`/`#error` so a rebase that removes or renames the upstream ID fails at compile time — an extra safety net on top of `check_chromium_src.py`.

choices: Nothing — `ChromeTypographyProvider` is the upstream class, so it's correct
It should call `BraveProvider::GetColor(id)` recursively
It should use `Super::GetColor(id)`
It should call `ChromiumImpl::GetColor(id)`
explain: Fallback methods must call the correct base class. With `#define` renames changing the hierarchy, the upstream implementation is `ChromiumImpl`, not the original class name.
